This repository's own operating rules (docs/OPERATING_RULES.md) were written specifically because an earlier pass in this same session discarded exactly this kind of access-terms workaround (a proxy bypass for a BAILII block, on the Contract Law and GCHQ files) rather than rely on it. Consistent with that precedent, this file does NOT rely on the agent's proxy-obtained pinpoint quotes or paragraph numbers as verified text. Instead, only the substance independently corroborated this session via a legitimate WebSearch of a genuine academic secondary source (Keith Stanton's peer-reviewed article 'Comparative Law in the House of Lords and Supreme Court') is used, and the entry is recorded at a correspondingly lower verification tier. This is a single-node entry: no clean statute pairs with this common-law methodological doctrine, and the researching agent itself recommended a 1-node framing given no second case was independently verified this session.

authorities.name: Fairchild v Glenhaven Funeral Services Ltd
authorities.date_note: Neutral citation date per the researching agent's account (a second source gave 16 May 2002 as the hearing/decision date) - not independently resolved to the exact day this session, since the case could not be reached through a route this file relies on for pinpoint accuracy.
authorities.proposition: Where English authority did not cleanly resolve a genuinely novel causation problem - multiple employers each in breach of duty, with scientific uncertainty over which exposure actually caused the claimant's mesothelioma - the House of Lords treated a comparative survey of how other legal systems handle the same evidential problem as a legitimate and persuasive aid to developing the common law, without treating any foreign rule as binding. Per Stanton's independently-corroborated academic account, the House of Lords unusually took the initiative to request comparative material mid-hearing, and was referred to German law (BGB s.830, which apportions liability among multiple actors where it cannot be established which one caused the harm) and a broader European survey (via van Gerven's Ius Commune casebook and the European Group on Tort Law's collection). Lord Bingham's own reasoning is reported (though not independently primary-verified this session) to have observed that there is no single universal test of causation, and that it would be contrary to principle to insist on a rule that yielded unfair results.
